title: NAD+ and Longevity in Brisbane: Why Levels Fall and Where Infusions Fit
standfirst: Levels of NAD+, a coenzyme central to energy and DNA repair, fall as we age. That is why longevity medicine takes an interest in it, though the case for infusions in people is still being made.
html:
NAD+ falls as we age. Research suggests that by your 50s it may be less than half of what it was in your 20s, and the decline is associated with many of the hallmarks of ageing: reduced energy, slower recovery, cognitive changes and greater susceptibility to age-related conditions.

That matters because nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, to give NAD+ its full name, is a coenzyme found in every cell of the body. It is central to energy metabolism, DNA repair, gene expression and the regulation of cellular stress responses. Without enough of it, cells cannot produce energy efficiently or repair damaged DNA, and cannot maintain the signalling pathways that keep tissues healthy.

The proteins that depend on NAD+

Sirtuins are a group of proteins that need NAD+ to work. They are sometimes nicknamed the body's "longevity genes". They regulate inflammation, mitochondrial function, DNA repair and cell survival pathways, and when NAD+ declines, sirtuin activity drops and the processes they regulate start to work less well.

PARP enzymes need NAD+ as well, to detect and repair breaks in DNA strands. As we age and DNA damage from environmental stressors builds up, PARPs consume more and more NAD+, which leaves less for energy production and other vital functions.

Research on NAD+ precursors and on direct NAD+ supplementation has grown substantially over the past decade, with studies examining a possible role in metabolic health, neurological function, cardiovascular health and overall cellular resilience.

What NAD+ does, and what is known about infusions

People often ask whether infusions help with energy, recovery, sleep, mood or ageing itself. The table sets what NAD+ does in the cell beside what can fairly be said about infusions. Every treatment at the clinic is individually assessed.

AreaWhat NAD+ does in the cellWhat can be said about infusions
Energy and mental clarityDirectly involved in mitochondrial energy productionIndividual responses vary and are not guaranteed
Recovery and physical performanceSupports muscle cell repair and mitochondrial function, both critical for physical recoverySome athletes and active people use it in their recovery routines; the evidence that infusions speed recovery is limited
Sleep qualityPlays a role in circadian rhythm regulationIndividual responses vary
Mood and neurological supportInvolved in the pathways that make neurotransmitters, and supports energy metabolism in nerve cellsEmerging research is examining a possible role in mood regulation and neurological resilience
Cellular longevitySupports sirtuin activity and DNA repair mechanismsThis is the reasoning behind its use in longevity medicine; infusions have not been shown to slow ageing in people

IV or oral NMN and NR?

Oral precursors such as NMN (nicotinamide mononucleotide) and NR (nicotinamide riboside) are widely available and can support NAD+ levels over time. An infusion delivers NAD+ directly into the bloodstream, bypassing the digestive tract, and reaches significantly higher plasma concentrations than oral supplements. If IV delivery is clinically indicated for you, your doctor will discuss the most appropriate approach.

What a course involves

At the clinic, NAD+ infusion therapy is part of a personalised longevity and wellness program, assessed and supervised by registered medical practitioners. It begins with a comprehensive medical consultation. A doctor reviews your health history and medicines alongside your current symptoms and goals, decides whether NAD+ is appropriate for you and, if it is, designs a personalised protocol.

Infusions are given at 628 Ipswich Road, Annerley, and typically take 1.5 to 3 hours, because the rate has to be carefully controlled to minimise side effects. Some patients notice mild sensations during the infusion, such as warmth or chest tightness, or nausea. These resolve when the rate is slowed, and the medical team monitors every patient throughout.

A typical initial course is 3 to 5 infusions over one to two weeks, followed by maintenance infusions as your treating doctor recommends.

Who it may suit, and who should not have it

NAD+ infusion therapy may be appropriate for people with:

  • persistent fatigue or low energy that has not responded to other interventions
  • cognitive changes associated with ageing or chronic stress
  • reduced physical performance or slow recovery from exercise
  • a proactive interest in longevity medicine and cellular health

People with a neurodegenerative condition sometimes ask about it too. That is assessed on an individual basis, and the evidence in these conditions is still early.

A thorough medical assessment is always required before treatment, because NAD+ therapy is not suitable for everyone. Certain medical conditions, including active cancer, pregnancy or specific cardiovascular conditions, may mean it is not appropriate for you.

structural_changes: Dropped the opening heading and opened on the age-related decline before defining the molecule, so this piece does not mirror the infusion-benefits article, which opens on the definition.
Recast the science section around the competition for NAD+ (sirtuins and PARPs drawing on a shrinking pool) and dropped the 'essential fuel' metaphor and the 'function optimally' line.

Replaced the five bold-label 'Potential Benefits' mini-sections with one table that puts what NAD+ does in the cell beside what can be said about infusions, so the molecule science stays and the infusion claims are visibly separate.
Kept the IV-versus-oral material as a deliberately short section under a specific heading ('IV or oral NMN and NR?').
Merged the clinic intro line into 'What a course involves', which now carries all the practical figures.
Moved 'neurodegenerative conditions' out of the 'may be appropriate' list into its own sentence with an evidence caveat.

Cut the 'Book a NAD+ Consultation' close ('specialises in longevity medicine', 'we invite you to book', 'a program tailored specifically to your health goals'); the piece now ends on who should not have it.
Removed 'It is important to note' and the three repeated 'individual responses vary' openers, keeping that caveat in the two table rows where the source placed it.
softened_claims: 'sirtuins – often referred to as the body's "longevity genes"' -> 'sometimes nicknamed the body's "longevity genes"'

'NAD+ is the essential fuel for ... sirtuins ... When NAD+ levels are sufficient, sirtuins function optimally' -> 'Sirtuins are a group of proteins that need NAD+ to work' ('function optimally' removed)

'By supporting sirtuin activity and DNA repair mechanisms, NAD+ therapy is considered a foundational component of a comprehensive longevity medicine approach' -> 'This is the reasoning behind its use in longevity medicine; infusions have not been shown to slow ageing in people'

'Athletes and active individuals often incorporate NAD+ therapy into their recovery protocols' -> 'Some athletes and active people use it in their recovery routines; the evidence that infusions speed recovery is limited'
'NAD+ is a precursor to neurotransmitter synthesis pathways' -> 'Involved in the pathways that make neurotransmitters'

'Neurodegenerative conditions (assessed on an individual basis)' listed under 'may be appropriate for' -> 'People with a neurodegenerative condition sometimes ask about it too. That is assessed on an individual basis, and the evidence in these conditions is still early.'

Standfirst 'Discover how NAD+ infusion therapy supports cellular energy, DNA repair, and healthy ageing' -> 'That is why longevity medicine takes an interest in it, though the case for infusions in people is still being made'
audit.facts_checked: Preserved: the 50s versus 20s 'less than half' estimate, the sirtuin and PARP science, NMN and NR supporting levels over time, significantly higher plasma concentrations with IV, 1.5 to 3 hours, the side effects (warmth, chest tightness, nausea) resolving when the rate is slowed, monitoring throughout, 3 to 5 infusions over one to two weeks then maintenance, the four remaining suitability items, and the exclusions (active cancer, pregnancy, specific cardiovascular conditions) with the assessment requirement. This article's 1.5 to 3 hours and 3 to 5 infusions differ from the other NAD+ articles (2 to 4 hours; 2 to 4 infusions over 2 to 4 weeks); kept as written, not resolved.
editor_notes: Removed 'patients commonly report improvements' (testimonial framing, restricted by AHPRA's advertising guidelines); the table is unchanged.
